source_book: NCERT Mathematics Class 12, Chapter 7 'Integrals' — chapter-index scope reference only; teaching, examples and phrasing authored from first principles. IB DP Analysis and Approaches guide (SL/HL), AP Calculus AB/BC CED, Cambridge IGCSE Additional Mathematics 0606 syllabus (limit-of-a-sum absence noted) and A-level Pure Mathematics specifications consulted for COVERAGE SCOPE only (curriculum_tags). constraints: f(x) = x^2 - c is a polynomial: defined and continuous for EVERY real x, on every value of c the sim ever reaches (c in [0,1]) -- there is no excluded point anywhere in the function's own domain

the DRAWN interval is x in [0, b] with b in [0.2, 2.0], authored as function_plot.x_domain = {min:0, max_expr:'b'} in every state except STATE_1's reveal window (max_expr:'min(xdraw, b)', handing off to 'b' with no discontinuity since xdraw's ceiling equals b's own static value at STATE_1's default 2.0)
gap(n) = b^3(3n-1)/(6n^2) is EXACT, strictly positive for every integer n >= 1, and is INDEPENDENT of c -- at STATE_4's fixed b=2, c=0 this is 4/n - 4/(3n^2), the founder-ratified F2 surface

tts_sentences.text_en: The curve draws left to right, then the region beneath it fills in completely — y equals x squared, bounding one exact area not yet measured.
A speed graph works this way too: the area under it is the distance the vehicle travelled.
Four rectangles estimate the region's area, each as tall as the curve where it begins.
Each rectangle's area is its width times its height, and its height is the curve's value at its left edge — which for the first one is zero.
Watch the rectangles multiply and thin, from just four toward a thousand — pausing at twenty, then again at a hundred.
Each time, the estimate climbs closer to a single number: the exact total the region is heading for, though the sum itself never actually reaches it.

misconception_watch.belief: Adding up rectangles is only ever an approximation, so the exact area is a fiction
misconception_watch.visual_counter: the picture stops moving at ten thousand rectangles but the gap number does not reach zero; its exact value, four over n minus four over three n squared, stays positive at every n
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: No count of rectangles reaches it — the integral is the number they head for.

tts_sentences.text_en: The picture stops moving, but the numbers do not.
Zoom into the last sliver: even at ten thousand rectangles, it is still there.
Its exact size is four over n, minus four over three n squared — always positive.
No count of rectangles ever makes that gap zero.

misconception_watch.belief: Area is a size, so it is always positive; an integral cannot be negative
misconception_watch.visual_counter: the dim chip reads total area = 2.0000 first, then the bright true total reads the integral = 0.6667, with the below-axis rectangles drawn downward and their subtotal minus 0.6667
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: Below the axis, the rectangle's height is negative — it subtracts.

tts_sentences.text_en: Lower the curve: part of it dips below the axis.
If area only ever added, the total would read 2.0000 — dim, and wrong here.
The real total is 0.6667, bright: the below-axis piece, minus 0.6667, subtracted from what is above.

misconception_watch.belief: Left rectangles and right rectangles give different answers, so one of them must be the wrong method
misconception_watch.visual_counter: at n equal to 8 all three sums appear together — 2.1875, 2.65625, 3.1875 — all correct, all different; as n grows the three readouts draw closer without ever landing on the same value
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: The sampling rule changes every finite sum and not the limit.

tts_sentences.text_en: Three rules sample the same rectangles differently: left sum (left Riemann sum), right sum, and midpoint.
Because this curve keeps rising, left stays smallest and right stays largest — three different numbers, bracketing the truth.
Add more rectangles: all three readouts draw closer, never landing on exactly the same value.

STATE_7.title: The Area So Far Is a Function

tts_sentences.text_en: Sweep the upper bound rightward: the filled region grows, and its running total is traced at the same moment as a new curve, A of x, the area swept so far.
By x equals 2, that curve ends at 2.6667 — the same number the rectangles were heading for all along.

aha_moment.statement: A pile of rectangles becomes the exact area — you can watch it happen.
aha_moment.visual_confirmation: the estimate Sₙ climbs from 1.7500 toward 2.6667 as the rectangle count grows from 4 to 1000

regeneration_variants.label: Same idea, a cubic curve
regeneration_variants.physical_world: the curve f(x) = x³ instead of x² − c
regeneration_variants.same_physics: rectangles still converge to one exact total as n grows, the gap still shrinks toward zero without reaching it, and the running accumulation is still a new function of the stopping point — only the closed forms change (the exact total becomes b⁴/4, the accumulation function becomes x⁴/4)
regeneration_variants.scene_hint: swap every function_plot / region_fill / riemann_bars y_expr from 'x*x - c' to 'x*x*x', and recompute the exact/gap/accumulation closed forms from the cubic's own antiderivative

regeneration_variants.label: Total rainfall from a rate graph
regeneration_variants.physical_world: a rainfall-rate-against-time graph instead of y = x² − c
regeneration_variants.same_physics: the area under a rate graph is still the accumulated total — rectangles built from the rate at each moment still converge to the exact total rainfall as the time-slices get thinner
regeneration_variants.scene_hint: relabel the axes 'time' and 'rainfall rate'; keep the same curve shape so every taught number stays unchanged

assessment.mastery_definition: A student has mastered this concept when they can estimate a definite integral with a small number of rectangles, explain why refining the partition makes the sum settle on one exact number rather than reaching it at any finite n, state the closed-form size of the left-sum gap and why it is never exactly zero, determine the sign of a definite integral when the curve dips below the axis and distinguish it from the total unsigned area, explain why left, right and midpoint sums differ at every finite n but converge to the same limit, and evaluate a simple accumulation function at a given point.

questions.stem: Estimate ∫₀¹ x² dx with 2 left rectangles.

distractor_misconceptions.B: computes the right sum instead of the specified left sum
distractor_misconceptions.C: samples at each interval's midpoint instead of its left edge
distractor_misconceptions.D: averages the left and right sums (the trapezium rule) instead of using the left sum alone

questions.tested_idea: the left Riemann sum samples the height at each subinterval's left edge, not its right edge, midpoint, or an average of both
questions.parallel_form_stem: Estimate ∫₀² x² dx with 2 left rectangles.

questions.stem: As n grows with the interval fixed, the sum Sₙ …

options.D: reaches the exact value at some finite n and then stays exactly there

distractor_misconceptions.B: assumes more rectangles always means an ever-larger sum, rather than a sum converging to a fixed total
distractor_misconceptions.C: invents oscillation with no basis in a steadily refining left-sum sequence for an increasing function
distractor_misconceptions.D: treats approaching a limit as eventually arriving at it exactly — the 'approaching is not reaching' misconception

questions.tested_idea: as n grows without bound, the sequence of Riemann sums converges to one fixed number, the exact integral, without ever exactly reaching it at any finite n
questions.parallel_form_stem: For a different increasing curve on a fixed interval, as n grows, does the left sum ever exceed the exact integral?

questions.stem: The left-sum gap on [0,2] behaves like 4/n; at n = 200 it is about …

distractor_misconceptions.B: believes a large enough n makes the gap reach exactly zero — the exact belief this state confronts
distractor_misconceptions.C: misplaces the decimal point by a factor of ten
distractor_misconceptions.D: misplaces the decimal point by a factor of one hundred

questions.tested_idea: the gap shrinks toward zero but is strictly positive at every finite n — never exactly zero
questions.parallel_form_stem: The same gap formula at n = 500 is about …

questions.stem: Is ∫₀² (x² − 2) dx positive, negative, or zero?

distractor_misconceptions.B: treats the integral as an area, which is always positive, instead of a signed total that can be negative
distractor_misconceptions.C: assumes the positive and negative parts must cancel exactly for any curve, not just a symmetric one
distractor_misconceptions.D: mistakes a negative result for an undefined one — the integrand is a polynomial, defined everywhere

questions.tested_idea: when a curve dips below the axis, the definite integral subtracts that piece — the signed total can be negative
questions.parallel_form_stem: Is ∫₀¹ (x² − 1) dx positive, negative, or zero?

questions.stem: For an increasing function, which of left, right or midpoint gives the largest sum?

distractor_misconceptions.B: swaps which edge over-estimates and which under-estimates for an increasing function
distractor_misconceptions.C: assumes the midpoint sum, not the right sum, gives the largest estimate for an increasing function
distractor_misconceptions.D: believes the three sampling rules must agree at every finite n instead of only in the limit

questions.tested_idea: for an increasing function, the right sum over-estimates, the left sum under-estimates, and the midpoint sum sits between them, at every finite n
questions.parallel_form_stem: For a decreasing function, which of left, right or midpoint gives the smallest sum?

questions.stem: If A(x) is the area from 0 to x under y = x², what is A(3)?

distractor_misconceptions.B: computes 3³ (27) and forgets to divide by 3
distractor_misconceptions.C: reports the upper bound itself instead of evaluating the accumulation function there
distractor_misconceptions.D: computes 3³/3 incorrectly instead of dividing 27 by 3

questions.tested_idea: the accumulation function A(x) = x³/3 is evaluated by substituting the given x — A(3) = 27/3 = 9
questions.parallel_form_stem: If A(x) is the area from 0 to x under y = x², what is A(2)?
